title: LightSwitch – In-Network and Photonic LLM Inference in Transit
content:
"Do not send data to centralized AI data centers: embed intelligence directly into the light traveling through global networks."
📖 Languages: English | 🇮🇹 Leggi in Italiano (Italian Version)
Project LightSwitch is an experimental software prototype and hardware architecture for In-Network & Photonic Artificial Intelligence Compute. It simulates executing Large Language Model (LLM) inference and matrix transformations directly inside optical fibers, switching cabins, and satellite laser links while packets are in transit, eliminating the GPU Von Neumann memory bottleneck and reducing compute energy by 
[ CLIENT (Copper / Wi-Fi) ] 
       ↓ (Tokenized prompt)
[ SWITCHING CABIN / EDGE PoP (P4 Switch / FPGA) ] ➔ Computes Initial Model Layers (15 ns)
       ↓ (WDM Optical Carrier Modulation @ 1550nm C-Band)
[ TERRESTRIAL & SUBMARINE OPTICAL FIBER ] ➔ Photons travel at 200,000 km/s in silica
       ↓ (Ternary Optical Phase Interference {-1, 0, 1})
[ LEO SATELLITE CONSTELLATION ] ➔ Inter-satellite laser links at 300,000 km/s (Speed of light in vacuum)
       ↓ (Downlink & Token Decapsulation)
[ DESTINATION GATEWAY ] ➔ Final output token already computed upon arrival! (Zero GPU queue latency)
- 
Zero Multiplications ($100%$ Additive Transforms): Model weights are quantized to 1.58-bit (${-1, 0, 1}$ ). Floating-point multiplications are replaced by optical constructive/destructive phase interference ($0\text{ FP Multiplications}$ ).
- 
Eliminating the Softmax Bottleneck: Integrates State-Space Models (Mamba / RWKV Linear SSMs) to compute recurrence ($h_t = Ah_{t-1} + Bx_t$ ) without$\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ Softmax in-flight.
- 
Physical Noise Resilience: Employs ITU-T G.709 Forward Error Correction (FEC) ensuring Post-FEC Bit Error Rate $\text{BER} < 10^{-15}$ across thousands of kilometers.
- 
Hyperscale Data Center Spine-Leaf Fabric: Applicable immediately inside private Big Tech AI Campus networks, cutting intra-datacenter optical transceiver energy by $>80%$ .
- 
Sub-2 Nanosecond Hardware Packet Filter: Switches inspect incoming headers in $< 1.5\text{ ns}$ , instantly distinguishing AI prompt packets from everyday Internet traffic (Netflix, Zoom, HTTPS).
- Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) Readiness: Can be deployed immediately using accessible hardware: AMD Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA SmartNICs (~€2,800) or Intel Tofino 2 P4 Switches (~€8,500).

report.summary: Open-source prototype embeds LLM inference directly into optical network light, using photonic phase interference to eliminate GPU bottlenecks and achieve in-transit compute.
report.background: Modern AI relies on massive centralized data centers filled with GPUs, creating energy-hungry systems with severe memory bottlenecks. Von Neumann architecture separates memory and processing, forcing constant data movement that dominates LLM inference costs. LightSwitch explores an alternative: perform computation while data travels through optical fiber and satellite links. It uses a 1.58-bit ternary representation ({-1, 0, 1}) to replace floating-point multiplications with additive optical interference, cutting multiplications to zero. The project integrates linear state-space models like Mamba and RWKV to avoid softmax bottlenecks, and employs forward error correction for long-distance resilience. It targets near-term deployment with commercial off-the-shelf hardware such as AMD Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGAs and Intel Tofino P4 switches, simulating an in-network pipeline from edge cabins through submarine fiber to LEO satellite constellations.
key_points: LightSwitch replaces traditional floating-point multiplication with optical phase interference. Model weights are quantized to 1.58 bits, meaning they only take values -1, 0, or 1. This eliminates all multiplications during inference, reducing computation to additive transforms that can be performed naturally by light waves interfering constructively or destructively in optical fiber.

The architecture executes LLM layers in transit inside network equipment. P4 switches and FPGAs at edge points compute initial model layers, then residual layers are processed via WDM optical carrier modulation along terrestrial and submarine fibers. By the time a token reaches its destination gateway, the output is already computed, theoretically removing GPU queue latency.

It sidesteps the softmax attention bottleneck by using state-space models instead of transformers. Linear recurrence equations like h_t = Ah_{t-1} + Bx_t allow sequential processing without O(N^2) softmax attention complexity. This makes in-flight, streamable inference more feasible across distributed optical hardware.

The project emphasizes practical, near-term deployment using COTS components. Estimated costs are roughly €2,800 for an FPGA SmartNIC or €8,500 for a Tofino 2 switch. The simulator includes real-world constraints like packet classification in under 1.5 nanoseconds, ITU-T G.709 forward error correction, and energy telemetry comparing against NVIDIA H100 servers.

A major claimed benefit is hyperscale data center spine-leaf efficiency. By moving compute into the optical fabric itself, LightSwitch expects to cut intra-datacenter optical transceiver energy by more than 80%. This could lower operational costs for big tech AI campuses without waiting for exotic new hardware.
report.impact: If LightSwitch proves viable, it could reshape AI infrastructure by making the network itself a massive distributed computer. Hyperscalers might reduce reliance on GPU clusters for inference, lowering energy costs and latency for global users. Developers would need new programming models targeting optical switches and FPGAs, but could benefit from near-zero queue delays and lower carbon footprints. Regular users would experience faster AI responses, particularly for global applications where data currently travels long distances to central clouds. However, the project is experimental: practical challenges like KV-cache storage, optical noise, and telecom integration remain substantial. Its greatest near-term impact may be as a research blueprint, inspiring hybrid approaches where optical accelerators complement rather than replace GPUs.
report.tools: Watch Project LightSwitch on GitHub (MIT licensed) for the full simulator, whitepapers, and hardware guides. For related technologies, explore Mamba and RWKV for linear state-space LLMs, Intel Tofino P4 switches and AMD Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGAs for programmable in-network compute, and Ollama for local LLM integration. Follow the repo's benchmarks and tests to understand the claimed energy and latency advantages.
